data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Ownership-based allocation systematically suppresses cross-cutting explanations, because it acts as an epistemic tariff: it protects the incumbent lineage's primitive vocabulary from being invalidated by rival primitives, causing the system to optimize for lineage-autarky rather than explanatory coverage.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If rival lineages universally converge on a complete universal grammar where all primitives are inter-derivable, then exclusion of L_rival primitives results in zero loss of representational power.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cost of translating or importing cross-cutting explanations across lineages exceeds the computational savings of ownership-based allocation, then the allocation is a net efficiency gain rather than suppression.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If cross-cutting explanations are systematically less robust than lineage-native explanations, their absence reflects a valid selection pressure rather than artificial suppression.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The reasoning system evaluates primitives using a local cost function bounded by the owning lineage's available vocabulary. When a problem is allocated to L_owner, rival primitives from L_rival are artificially excluded from the action space. This forces L_owner to construct an explanation using combinations of its own weaker primitives. Consequently, the search space is pruned of cross-cutting explanations (those requiring L_rival's primitives) not because they are suboptimal, but because they are unrepresentable in the allocated subspace.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
